The research demonstrates the critical role of universities and colleges in equipping students with the AI skills they will need to thrive in life beyond higher education. It also highlights the continuing risks AI poses for the effective assessment of students’ work and the credibility of qualifications, as well as the potential for AI to benefit higher education.

Many institutions continue to use unsupervised assessments that can be completed to a high standard using AI tools without substantive engagement from students. In the roundtable discussions and interviews that informed the research, students described peers who had completed assessments using large language models, sometimes in just a few minutes, and received a similar grade to those who had completed the assessment themselves. Staff participants raised concerns that assessments do not consistently and reliably assess students’ knowledge and skills.

The report highlights the importance of designing assessments that reliably demonstrate whether students have achieved the intended learning outcomes. In many cases, assessments designed to prevent AI use, such as closed-book exams, presentations, practical assessments and performances, are likely to provide the most valid measure of student attainment.

Discussions with students and staff also found that: 

  • Use of AI among teaching and professional services staff varies significantly, both within and between institutions. Some staff are developing innovative approaches, while others use AI rarely or not at all.
  • Many students use AI in sophisticated ways to support their studies. However, students and staff expressed concerns that some uses displace the cognitive effort required for deep learning.
  • Many students find their institution’s or department’s policies on AI difficult to understand. Some also felt that staff use of AI had reduced the quality of learning materials.
  • AI literacy training for staff is often limited and generally voluntary, with levels of participation typically low.
  • Students see AI literacy as important to their future employment prospects and would welcome more opportunities to develop AI skills.

Commenting on the research Josh Fleming, Director of Strategy and Delivery at the OfS, said:

‘AI is rapidly reshaping higher education. This is a huge opportunity for universities and colleges to leverage the technology for the benefit of students and society. We’ve seen fantastic examples of this opportunity being seized across the sector.

‘It also presents a generational risk to the system as it stands, threatening to undermine students' learning and institutions' ability to assess them. We need to see far greater efforts to tackle these risks, including far greater use of AI-free assessment.

‘The scale and pace of both the challenge and opportunity presents a novel challenge for the sector and us as the regulator. We will continue to work with universities and colleges to help them reap the benefits of AI while avoiding the risks.’

Commenting on the research, Kathryn Harrison-Graves, Deputy Chief Executive at Advance HE, said:

‘This research highlights the real energy and creativity across the sector, with staff and departments leading the way in exploring what AI can offer.

‘As institutions build on that work, there is a valuable opportunity to bring it together under a clear institutional direction. Students told us they would welcome greater clarity about what is expected of them, and staff are approaching AI with varying levels of confidence and support.

‘Senior leaders are well placed to help by setting a shared vision for AI, supporting consistent and well communicated guidance, and making time, training and resources available to staff and students. Regular discussion at executive and board level, alongside giving staff the confidence to make good decisions in the interests of their students, will help institutions make the most of this work.’

In response to the research findings, the OfS will:

  • Require institutions to ensure assessments are valid and reliable measures of students’ knowledge and skills. In many cases, this will require the use of secure (AI-free) assessments. Institutions must also ensure courses are up-to-date and require students to develop relevant skills. Alongside the report, we have set out how institutions can comply with our regulation in the context of AI.
  • Hold institutions to account when they fall short. Where evidence suggests institutions have not met our requirements, we deploy our regulatory levers, which include imposing specific conditions of registration, monetary penalties or suspending access to student support funding and/or OfS grant funding.
  • Support universities and colleges to strengthen their approaches to AI, including by clarifying how OfS regulatory requirements apply in the context of AI and sharing examples of effective practice.
  • Continue to deepen sector understanding of how AI is reshaping higher education by undertaking further structured research to establish the scale and nature of change.

In response to the findings, Advance HE will:

  • Launch an AI focused Change Academy programme for member institutions early in 2027. Designed as a peer-learning and action-learning programme connecting Advance HE members from across the globe, the Change Academy will create space for leaders to pause, reflect and develop their institutional AI strategy.  
  • Convene sector leaders, industry experts and academics to explore effective approaches to responding to AI within teaching and learning, leadership, governance and inclusion.
  • Continually review frameworks and resources available to members via the Advance HE Knowledge Hub to provide guidance and shape discussion around ethical and appropriate use of AI in higher education.

translation.html:
这项研究表明，大学和学院在帮助学生掌握走出高等教育后在人生中取得成功所需的 AI 技能方面发挥着关键作用。研究还强调，AI 持续给学生作业的有效评估和学历资格的公信力带来风险，同时也有潜力为高等教育带来益处。

许多院校仍在采用无监考考核，学生无需实质性参与，使用 AI 工具就能高质量完成。在为这项研究提供依据的圆桌讨论和访谈中，学生提到，有同学使用大语言模型完成考核，有时只需几分钟，就获得了与独立完成考核的学生相近的成绩。参与研究的教职员工担心，现有考核无法始终如一、可靠地评估学生的知识和技能。

报告强调，考核设计必须能够可靠地证明学生是否达到了预期学习成果。在许多情况下，为防止使用 AI 而设计的考核，例如闭卷考试、演示汇报、实践考核和表演，可能最能有效衡量学生的学习成就。

与学生和教职员工的讨论还发现： 

  • 教学人员和专业服务人员使用 AI 的情况差异显著，同一院校内部及不同院校之间均是如此。一些员工正在探索创新做法，另一些则很少使用或完全不使用 AI。
  • 许多学生以成熟、灵活的方式使用 AI 辅助学习。不过，学生和教职员工都担心，某些使用方式取代了深度学习所需的认知努力。
  • 许多学生觉得，所在院校或院系的 AI 政策难以理解。一些学生还认为，教职员工使用 AI 降低了学习材料的质量。
  • 面向教职员工的 AI 素养培训往往有限，而且通常采取自愿参加的方式，参与率普遍较低。
  • 学生认为 AI 素养对未来就业前景很重要，并希望有更多机会培养 AI 技能。

英国学生事务办公室（OfS）战略与执行总监 Josh Fleming 在评论这项研究时表示：

“AI 正在迅速重塑高等教育。这为大学和学院利用这项技术造福学生和社会提供了巨大机遇。我们已在整个高等教育领域看到许多抓住这一机遇的出色案例。

“它也给现行体系带来了影响一代人的风险，可能削弱学生的学习成效和院校评估学生的能力。我们需要看到力度大得多的行动来应对这些风险，包括大幅增加不使用 AI 的考核。

“这些挑战和机遇的规模与发展速度，给高等教育领域以及作为监管机构的我们带来了前所未有的挑战。我们将继续与大学和学院合作，帮助它们在规避风险的同时获得 AI 带来的益处。”

Advance HE 副首席执行官 Kathryn Harrison-Graves 在评论这项研究时表示：

“这项研究凸显了整个高等教育领域切实展现出的活力和创造力，教职员工和各部门正带头探索 AI 能够带来什么。

“随着院校在这些工作的基础上继续推进，一个宝贵的机会是，在明确的院校整体方向下统筹这些工作。学生告诉我们，他们希望更清楚地了解学校对自己的要求，而教职员工在运用 AI 时的信心水平和获得的支持各不相同。

“高层领导能够发挥重要作用，包括确立共同的 AI 愿景，支持制定一致且传达清晰的指导，并为教职员工和学生提供时间、培训和资源。在管理层和理事会层面定期开展讨论，同时让教职员工有信心作出符合学生利益的明智决策，将帮助院校充分发挥这些工作的价值。”

针对研究结果，OfS 将：

  • 要求院校确保考核能够有效、可靠地衡量学生的知识和技能。在许多情况下，这将要求采用有保障的（不使用 AI 的）考核。院校还必须确保课程与时俱进，并要求学生培养相关技能。随报告一同发布的还有我们对院校如何在 AI 背景下遵守我们的监管要求的说明。
  • 对未达标的院校追究责任。如果有证据表明院校未满足我们的要求，我们会运用监管手段，包括施加特定的注册条件、处以罚款，或暂停其获取学生资助资金和／或 OfS 拨款的资格。
  • 支持大学和学院加强其 AI 应对方式，包括明确 OfS 监管要求在 AI 背景下如何适用，以及分享有效实践案例。
  • 继续开展进一步的系统性研究，确定变化的规模和性质，加深高等教育领域对 AI 如何重塑高等教育的认识。

针对研究结果，Advance HE 将：

  • 于 2027 年初为成员院校推出聚焦 AI 的 Change Academy 项目。Change Academy 被设计为一项连接全球 Advance HE 成员的同伴学习和行动学习项目，将为领导者创造空间，让他们暂缓脚步、进行反思，并制定所在院校的 AI 战略。  
  • 召集高等教育领域的领导者、行业专家和学者，探讨在教学与学习、领导力、治理和包容性方面应对 AI 的有效方法。
  • 持续审查通过 Advance HE Knowledge Hub 向成员提供的框架和资源，为高等教育中合乎伦理且恰当地使用 AI 提供指导，并引导相关讨论。
